own_scenes.desc: Una mano izquierda insistente que repite patrones sobre los acordes del blues mientras la derecha sincopa melodías o acordes en bloque: exige independencia entre las manos. El nombre aparece a finales de los años veinte, quizá por un baile (lo sugiere el comentario de Pine Top Smith en su «Pine Top's Boogie Woogie»), y el estilo vive entre el blues y el jazz, sobre todo como piano solo o a dúos y tríos (Meade Lux Lewis, Albert Ammons, Pete Johnson). Hacia 1940 lo adoptan las grandes bandas de swing y hasta las Andrews Sisters.

refs.q: La esencia de este estilo consistía en el insistente empleo en la mano izquierda de patrones basados en sucesiones de acordes de blues
refs.para: El desarrollo del boogie-woogie durante los años veinte y treinta, que culminaría con el auge de su popularidad en torno a 1940, vino a ampliar aún más el vocabulario del piano afroamericano. La esencia de este estilo consistía en el insistente empleo en la mano izquierda de patrones basados en sucesiones de acordes de blues, los cuales subrayaban las líneas melódicas sincopadas o acordes en bloques de la mano derecha. Este contraste exigía al pianista una hábil independencia entre las manos. El término «boogie-woogie» se empezó a utilizar por primera vez a finales de los años veinte (aunque es posible que las raíces de este estilo datasen de finales del siglo XIX), y quizá se aplicase originalmente a una danza que fuera acompañada por esta bulliciosa música de piano (así lo da a entender, por ejemplo, el comentario hablado de Pine Top Smith en «Pine Top’s Boogie Woogie», de 1928). Sin embargo, el estilo alcanzaría su máxima expresión como música de teclado sin acompañamiento, aunque no era infrecuente que los pianistas interpretaran juntos en dúos y tríos, como en «Boogie Woogie Prayer», grabado por Meade Lux Lewis, Albert Ammons y Pete Johnson. Algunos de los principales representantes de este estilo tocaban ocasionalmente otros estilos de jazz, pero mayoritariamente el boogie-woogie conservó su carácter de música tangencial, ubicada en los intersticios existentes entre el blues y el jazz. El estilo alcanzó su máxima popularidad durante la era del swing, cuando fue adoptado por gran número de intérpretes del mainstream, como Tommy Dorsey en «Boogie Woogie» (1938), Count…

podcast.title: Revival and Mainstream Popularity (1938)
podcast.body: By 1938, Boogie Woogie had somewhat fallen out of fashion after a brief popularity a decade earlier. However, the "Spirituals to Swing" concerts organized by John Hammond, featuring artists like Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons, dramatically changed this. Suddenly, Boogie Woogie became "the biggest thing in music," leading every big band to adapt it to their style, and its influence appeared in numerous popular songs of the early 1940s. "That show changed that, and suddenly Boogie Woogie was the biggest thing in music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dissemination via Radio (WWII Era)
podcast.body: Boogie-Woogie was one of several new sounds, including Jump Blues, Swing, Gospel, and Spear Trolls, that became part of a "melting pot" of music disseminated through radio during World War II. This was a direct result of the problems faced by Big Bands and the American Federation of Musicians strike, which opened airwaves to diverse genres. "Boogie-Wooogie, Jump Blues, Swing, Gospel, Spear Trolls, a whole new melting pot of sounds was created and disseminated through the radio as a result of the big band problems and the musician's strike."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fats Domino's Signature Style
podcast.body: Fats Domino was celebrated for his unique Boogie Woogie piano style, which was characterized by its reliance on triplets rather than the more conventional, straightforward rhythms often used by other pianists. "He was known as one of the best Boogie Boogie players around, with a unique style based on triplets, rather than the more straightforward rhythms many Boogie pianists used."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Historical Racist Criticism
podcast.body: Boogie-Woogie was targeted in a British newspaper review which described it as deplorable and tribal, originating from America and stemming from the "jungle," suggesting it might be "the Negro's revenge." This criticism also linked boogie-woogie with other genres like ragtime, blues, jazz, and hot cha-cha under the same racist condemnation in 1956. "It follows ragtime, blues, jazz, hot cha-cha, and the boogie-woogie, which surely originated in the jungle. We sometimes wonder whether this is the Negro's revenge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Piano Playing Style
podcast.body: Boogie Woogie is a distinct style of piano playing that became popular in the 1930s. It is characterized by the left hand playing a strong, repeating bass line, often referred to as "eight to the bar," while the right hand plays decorative melodic passages over it. This bass line and melody combination became the cornerstone of rock piano playing, as well as influencing country music. "The left hand would play that, while the right hand would play decorative melodic stuff over it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
